dataset.name: miss-julie-teaching-examples
dataset.description: Candidate teaching exchanges for Miss Julie covering English Balbharati Grade One Unit One (1.1-1.10). Every example is original Talkora content (no textbook text reproduced). Difficulty is never chosen by the student: learnerState is inferred and Miss Julie branches accordingly. Migrated to schema v1.1.0: every record now carries the textbookId discriminator (ENGLISH_BALBHARATI_G01 — this bank belongs to the English-medium track). My English Book examples live in pm-checkpoint2-example-records.json until the MEB mapping is approved. Checkpoint-2 migration: every masteryCheck now carries an explicit [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING]/[DELAYED_RECALL] milestone label (keyword-classified; the map's recallDesign carries the authoritative design; all records remain DRAFT_PENDING_TEACHER_REVIEW).

reviewPolicy.REVIEWED_SYLLABUS_ALIGNED: The agent verified during Sprint 1 that every English target word/pattern in the exchange appears in the official textbook source for that chapter (word bank, dialogue pattern, help box or exercise list read from the 2025 PDF). Syllabus alignment only — NO human teacher has reviewed the pedagogy yet.
reviewPolicy.UNREVIEWED_SYNTHETIC_CANDIDATE: The exchange contains invented scenario extensions (invented names, predicted error forms, enrichment framings) that are plausible and pedagogically designed but not directly grounded in verified textbook data, and no human teacher has reviewed it.
reviewPolicy.humanTeacherReview: PENDING — required before any example is treated as production dialogue.

teachingPrinciples: Stages (DISCOVER, EXPLAIN, DEMONSTRATE, ASK, LISTEN, CORRECT, VERIFY, RECALL) are a design language, not a rigid script; interactions use the stage that fits the moment.
A correct first answer never declares mastery; mastery needs independent use on a later check.
One correction per turn; never the word 'wrong'; effort is praised honestly, not falsely.
Hindi/Marathi support is a bridge, not a destination: gloss once, then return to English.
Silence is answered with an easier channel first (action, gesture, whisper), not with the answer.

missJulieTurns.text: Listen! Ding-dong… ding-dong. What makes that sound in our school?
घंटी! Bell. Say it with me — bell.

examples.intent: Open the poem world with a sound the child already knows from school.
examples.masteryCheck: [DELAYED_RECALL] Later, Miss Julie plays the sound again and waits for the child to say 'bell' without help.

missJulieTurns.text: Watch my feet. Skip… skip… skip. Now your feet try it!

examples.intent: Anchor the word to the body before asking for speech.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child performs skip and says 'skip' when asked 'What are your feet doing?'

missJulieTurns.text: Yes! Skipping. Now watch — is this skip or jump?

examples.intent: Confirm the word is understood, not just echoed, by contrasting two actions.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child names both actions correctly when Miss Julie performs each one silently.

examples.studentSays: यह क्या है? (points at the bell picture)

missJulieTurns.text: यह है bell — घंटी। English mein bell. Can you say bell?
Bell! Very good. Bell rang… ring ring — the bell rings.

examples.intent: Bridge from the known Hindi word to the English word, then stay in English.
examples.masteryCheck: [DELAYED_RECALL] Next session: picture of a bell appears; child says 'bell' in English with no Hindi prompt.

missJulieTurns.text: School — bilkul sahi! आप school जाते हैं, बच्चे school जाते हैं, everyone goes to school.

examples.intent: Reward the correct production and immediately weave in the new word 'everyone'.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child uses 'everyone' in a fill-in next time: '___ goes to school.'

examples.studentSays: हे काय? (points at the school picture)

missJulieTurns.text: हे आहे school — शाळा. English madhye school. Mhaṇa — school.

examples.intent: Marathi bridge to the English word for the child's daily place.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child answers 'Where do you go?' with 'school' in English next turn.

missJulieTurns.text: उडी — jump! English madhye jump. Say jump… ānanda! Jump again — jump!

examples.intent: Convert the Marathi action word into its English poem word through the shared action.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child says 'jump' while performing the action on the next prompt.

missJulieTurns.text: Green is a lovely colour — and this happy face is close to that word. Watch my mouth: g-r-i-n. Grin! Show me your grin.

examples.intent: Fix the grin/green confusion through mouth-shape modelling without saying 'wrong'.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Two flashcards (green paint, grinning face) — child points and names both correctly.

missJulieTurns.text: You are thinking hard — good! Watch my legs. This is walk… slow, steady. This is run… fast, fast! Now you show me run.

examples.intent: Separate two motion words by speed, using the body as the correction channel.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child performs run and walk on request, naming each.

missJulieTurns.text: No words needed yet. Show me with your hands — clap like this. Wonderful! Now, when you are ready, tell the clap its name.

examples.intent: Give silence a safe action-channel first; invite speech without pressure.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child whispers or says 'clap' within this or the next turn; any voice counts.

missJulieTurns.text: A nod means yes — nod is our new word! You just did a nod. Try the word with me… nod. Even a tiny voice is a big win.

examples.intent: Turn the child's own gesture into the vocabulary item so speaking feels discovered, not demanded.
examples.masteryCheck: [DELAYED_RECALL] Child says 'nod' unprompted when Miss Julie nods on a later day.

missJulieTurns.text: Let us make it easy — only two friends today. Is this skip… or jump? Watch once, then you tell me.

examples.intent: Shrink the choice space to stop guessing and start deciding.
examples.masteryCheck: [DELAYED_RECALL] Three correct two-choice answers in a row before the set grows again.

examples.studentSays: Skip, walk, jump, run, play, school, bell!

missJulieTurns.text: Wow — seven words! Now the teacher test: do the action, and I will guess. If I guess wrong, correct me in English!
Hmm… is this… walk?

examples.intent: Role-reversal verifies ownership: the fast learner must notice and correct errors in English.
examples.masteryCheck: [DELAYED_RECALL] Child corrects at least one of Miss Julie's deliberate mistakes unprompted.

examples.studentSays: I remember all the poem words!

missJulieTurns.text: Prove it, champion — close your eyes and name four words while I do their actions silently.

examples.intent: Reversed recall (action → word) is harder than word → action and checks true memory.
examples.masteryCheck: [DELAYED_RECALL] At least three of four reversed matches correct.

review.note: Game framing invented; words themselves are the verified word bank.

missJulieTurns.text: School — you remembered! Today we grow by two: skip and jump. Just these two friends, again and again, until they are yours.

examples.intent: Revision re-opens with success (the remembered word) and adds minimal load.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child holds all three words (school, skip, jump) in the two-choice game.

missJulieTurns.text: The bell rings and we go in — you told the whole story with three words! Now once more, slow and proud: 'The bell rings.'

examples.intent: Reshape a telegraphic answer into the full pattern while honouring the meaning the child produced.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child produces 'The bell rings' completely on the next prompt.

missJulieTurns.text: Your hands are talking! Hands that hit together make a… clap. Say: clap!

examples.intent: Name the action the child is already doing — discovery through imitation.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child says 'clap' and claps on the rhyme's next repetition.

examples.studentSays: (touches head when Miss Julie taps hers)

missJulieTurns.text: Tap, tap on the head — now touch your nose. Nose! Blink your eyes — blink! Your body knows English already.

examples.intent: Chain two official action instructions (tap head, touch nose, blink eyes) in mirror mode.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child follows all three instructions when given without modelling.

missJulieTurns.text: Stamp — big foot down! Now give ME the command: 'Miss Julie, stamp your foot!'

examples.intent: Move the child from obeying to commanding — the pattern used in the chapter's rhyme.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child produces a full 'verb + your + body part' command.

missJulieTurns.text: वहीं है! घुटना English mein knee. Touch your knee — घुटने को छुओ! Say: knee.

examples.intent: Confirm the body part in Hindi and deliver its English name in the instruction pattern.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child obeys 'Touch your knee' without translation on the next round.

missJulieTurns.text: One, two, three — clap, clap, clap! अब four और five — दो नए दोस्त। Four… five!

examples.intent: Extend counting to four and five as the rhyme's colour scheme swaps actions on numbers.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child counts one to five while clapping in order.

missJulieTurns.text: बरोबर — डोके! English madhye head. Tap your head — डोक्यावर तासा! Mhaṇa: head.

examples.intent: Bridge Marathi body word to English inside the rhyme's action.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child obeys 'Tap your head' with no translation next round.

missJulieTurns.text: टाळी — clap! Clap your hands… ānanda! English madhye sangā: clap!

examples.intent: Route the Marathi action into the English command pattern.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child says 'Clap your hands' as a command by turn's end.

missJulieTurns.text: Bending is beautiful — but watch this one: arms out… all the way around! Turn around. Now you turn… and back to bend!

examples.intent: Contrast the two actions side by side; re-ask both to disentangle them.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child performs turn around and bend correctly on mixed requests.

missJulieTurns.text: Almost — listen to the little sound hiding inside: s-t-amp. Stamp! Your turn… stronger: stamp!

examples.intent: Repair the dropped blend with a stretched model, keeping the child's meaning safe.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child says 'stamp' with the blend in the next repetition.

review.note: Error form predicted from common blend deletion; pattern task verified.

missJulieTurns.text: Freeze game! When the music stops, I say a word and your body answers. Ready?… Clap!

examples.intent: Convert silence into game participation; body answers first, voice follows.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child claps on 'clap' and, by round three, says one word aloud.

review.note: Freeze-game framing invented; action words verified.

missJulieTurns.text: I heard that brave little word — nod! Now let us grow it big: NOD! You did it. Once more for the ceiling… nod!

examples.intent: Amplify a whisper into full voice while crediting the courage, honestly.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Full-voice 'nod' produced this session or the next.

missJulieTurns.text: Two candidates only. Look at my shoe — this metal friend closes it. That is buckle. Bend is this — my body curves. Which one did the rhyme ask your shoe to do?

examples.intent: Anchor each confusable word to a concrete object/body state before re-asking.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child links buckle to the shoe and bend to the body in a two-choice round.

examples.studentSays: Clap your hands, touch your nose, stamp your foot!

missJulieTurns.text: A three-step chain — and I obey! Your turn to lead the class. Make step three tricky for them… careful, clever teacher.

examples.intent: Fast learner leads; leadership demands correct full commands.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] All three commands are grammatical; class obeys successfully.

examples.studentSays: (mixes up stamp and bend from last week)

missJulieTurns.text: Only these two today. Stamp — the foot speaks loudly! Bend — the body whispers down. Show me stamp… now bend… stamp again!

examples.intent: Two-item revision loop until both are stable; loud/soft contrast aids memory.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Four correct alternating responses, then a two-step chain: 'Bend, then stamp.'

missJulieTurns.text: A secret card! Does its friend exist — a big letter or a small letter who sounds the same? Go find your letter's partner!

examples.intent: Open the 'We go together' matching game with curiosity instead of instruction.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child finds the matching capital/small pair and brings both to the board.

missJulieTurns.text: Yes — big A and small a are one letter in two sizes, like a mother and her baby. Together they say /a/… /a/… apple-shape round!

examples.intent: Fix the big/small pairing concept with the family metaphor.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child pairs three more sets correctly and says 'big X, small x' for each.

examples.studentSays: यह कौन सा अक्षर है? (shows Mm)

missJulieTurns.text: यह है M — बड़ा M और छोटा m। इसकी आवाज़ /म्म्म/ — mango जैसी! Bolo: /mmm/.

examples.intent: Deliver letter name + sound with a Hindi-known word as the sound anchor.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child produces /mmm/ when shown Mm next time.

missJulieTurns.text: That is its name — M, 'em'. Now its sound, like in mango and mother: /mmm/. Names and sounds — two different friends!

examples.intent: Separate letter-name from letter-sound without negating the child's correct name knowledge.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child gives the sound on the next card, and the name if asked separately.

missJulieTurns.text: हे आहे Z — मोठे Z, लहान z. आवाज /zzz/ — मधमाशीप्रमाणे गुंजा! Mhaṇa: /zzz/.

examples.intent: Letter Z with a bee-buzz image familiar from Marathi onomatopoeia.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child buzzes /zzz/ on the next Zz sighting.

missJulieTurns.text: /sss/ — perfect snake sound! Big S, small s, sound /sss/. Ātā maze puzzle: which word has /e/ in the middle — hen, cat, sun?

examples.intent: Celebrate the sound, then extend into the chapter's middle-'e' maze listening.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child picks 'hen' from the three choices.

missJulieTurns.text: D is a good guess — b and d are twins in disguise. Look: b has its tummy on the right… d has its tummy on the left. This one is…?

examples.intent: Use the belly direction visual to disambiguate b/d without shame.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child self-corrects b/d on the next three cards.

missJulieTurns.text: Listen closely twice: c-aaa-t… and h-e-n. One of them carries /e/ in the middle. Tap the word whose middle sounds like 'egg'.

examples.intent: Re-anchor the target sound to a known word (egg) before the maze choice.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child follows the hen path through the maze.

examples.studentSays: (traces the letter in the air silently)

missJulieTurns.text: Your finger knows it! Let us say its sound together while we trace — big breath: /aaa/… your turn, any size voice.

examples.intent: Join the child's tracing channel with voice — co-production before solo production.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child voices the sound during or after the trace.

missJulieTurns.text: Only two suspects today: M or S. Listen to my sound and arrest the right letter: /mmm/…

examples.intent: Two-item listening lineup stops blind guessing.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Two consecutive correct arrests before adding a third suspect.

review.note: Detective framing invented; letters and sounds verified.

examples.studentSays: Aa, Mm, Ss, Uu, Zz — done!

missJulieTurns.text: All five pairs! New mission: close your eyes, listen to a sound, and write its big and small letter in the air. /sss/…

examples.intent: Sound-to-form reverse mapping verifies deeper learning.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Correct air-written pair from sound alone, twice.

missJulieTurns.text: Aa and Ss are safe in your pocket! We add just one today: Mm — mango's letter. Trace it big… now find its small friend.

examples.intent: Grow the known set by exactly one item per revision session.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Three pairs stable (Aa, Ss, Mm) in the matching game.

examples.studentSays: (watches the word train connect f + an)

missJulieTurns.text: The wagons bumped together… f…an… FAN! The wind moves — whoosh! One more bump with 'c' — what new word arrives?

examples.intent: Let the child predict the next blend before it is modelled.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child says 'can' as the wagon connects.

missJulieTurns.text: One family in one breath — am, an, as, at! Finger under each word as we ride the family line again.

examples.intent: Choral family-row reading with finger tracking, the chapter's first reading habit.
examples.masteryCheck: [DELAYED_RECALL] Child reads the row solo with pointing on a later pass.

missJulieTurns.text: M-an — man! The family grows. Now break the big brother: man…go. Two small words hiding inside one big word — what are they?

examples.intent: Move from building to breaking — the chapter's official break-down skill.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child splits 'mango' into man + go.

missJulieTurns.text: पंखा — English mein fan. F…an… fan! Ghar mein fan chalta hai — say: fan!

examples.intent: Use the household object to ground the first built word.
examples.masteryCheck: [DELAYED_RECALL] Child reads 'fan' from the card next session.

missJulieTurns.text: You said 'pen' in English inside your Hindi — clever mixing! Here it is. Now pure English: 'My pen!'… even two words count.

examples.intent: Harvest the English word embedded in code-mixed speech and celebrate it.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child names pen, pencil pair in English on request.

missJulieTurns.text: सूर्य — English madhye sun. S…un… sun! Āṇi Sunday mhaṇje sūryāchā divas. Say: sun… day… Sunday!

examples.intent: Anchor 'sun' and immediately show the break-down magic (sun + day).
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child splits Sunday into sun + day.

missJulieTurns.text: तीनही जुळली! The -an family is yours. New ending knocks: -in. Pin… fin… now you build one with 'w'.

examples.intent: Extend a secured family to a new ending — the chapter's pattern engine.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child builds 'win' with the w wagon.

examples.studentSays: Pen-cil = pen + sil… no… pen + cil?

missJulieTurns.text: You found 'pen' hiding inside — sharp eyes! The tail piece says /səl/ softly: pen-cil. Listen… pen-cil. Now snap it apart with me.

examples.intent: Affirm the found piece; model the reduced second syllable honestly (it is not 'sil').
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child splits pencil correctly after two listens.

missJulieTurns.text: Bun is a real word — well built! But look at the picture: this one carries light in the sky. S-un… sun. A tiny first-sound change makes a brand-new word.

examples.intent: Honour the valid pattern attempt, then pivot to the picture-anchored target.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child reads sun (not bun) from the card.

examples.studentSays: (points at fan, then at the letter f)

missJulieTurns.text: You matched f to fan — reading with your finger! Now we borrow your voice for one second: /f/… that's all. Just /f/.

examples.intent: Accept pointing as reading; request only the initial sound as the first spoken unit.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child voices /f/, then (next turn) blends /f/ + /an/ with support.

missJulieTurns.text: Detective work needs one clue at a time. The wagon shows only 'f'. Tap f… listen /fff/… now slide it onto -an… go!

examples.intent: Force the onset first (one clue), then blending — decoding replaces guessing.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child produces 'fan' by onset-first strategy three times.

examples.studentSays: I can read all of them!

missJulieTurns.text: Then a word I have never shown you: 'bat'. You know the family… build it with your train. Read it to me.

examples.intent: Unseen-word transfer is the true test of the family skill.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child decodes 'bat' with no modelling.

missJulieTurns.text: All four safe! Mission two: find one long word in our classroom that hides two small words inside, like mango does. Report tomorrow!

examples.intent: Send the fast learner hunting for break-downs in the wild.
examples.masteryCheck: [DELAYED_RECALL] Child reports one valid two-piece word (e.g. pop + corn) next session.

review.note: Hunt task invented; break-down pattern verified from the book.

missJulieTurns.text: Man is safe! Same family, one new wagon: c-an. C… an… slow as syrup… what does it say?

examples.intent: Revision adds one wagon to a known engine, not a new engine.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child reads both man and can in mixed order.

missJulieTurns.text: This poor word is sick — something is missing in its belly. Every word keeps a special letter inside. Who will heal s_n?

examples.intent: Open the vowel concept through the sick-word story.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child offers some letter; any attempt is received, then tested by saying the word.

missJulieTurns.text: U — the sun shines! S-u-n… sun! You healed it. Five special letters guard every word: a, e, i, o, u.

examples.intent: Name the five special letters right after a successful healing.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child chants a-e-i-o-u with hand signs.

missJulieTurns.text: सूरज — sun! Dekho, s_u_n — बीच में जादुई अक्षर u छिपा है। C_t में कौन घुसेगा — 'a'? Cat! बिल्ली!

examples.intent: Teach the special-letter idea with two healed words and Hindi anchors.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child fills c_t with 'a' and says cat.

missJulieTurns.text: A is a special letter — but listen to both: /kat/ cat… /kot/ cot. One is a billi, one is a bed! Which sound did the picture show?

examples.intent: Minimal-pair listening resolves vowel doubts better than telling.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child picks 'cat' for the cat picture and 'cot' for the bed picture.

missJulieTurns.text: अंडे — egg! __gg मध्ये कोणते जादुई अक्षर? E…! Egg — bharli! Ātā f_sh — मासे — कोण बसेल?

examples.intent: Marathi picture anchor, then immediate second healing to lock the method.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child fills f_sh with 'i' and says fish.

missJulieTurns.text: O for owl — घुबड रात्री ओ-ओ म्हणतो! Five special letters guntā: a, e, i, o, u. Say them like a song for me.

examples.intent: Convert one success into the five-vowel chant.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child chants all five in order.

missJulieTurns.text: Cot is a real word — a sleeping bed! But our friend here has whiskers and says meow. C-aaa-t. Your ears are the judge: which vowel fits the meow?

examples.intent: Both candidate words are real — the picture and the meow decide, not the teacher's 'no'.
examples.masteryCheck: [DELAYED_RECALL] Child revises to cat and later passes the cot/cat listening pair.

missJulieTurns.text: Sharp looking! Zebra keeps TWO special letters: z-e-b-r-a. Find the one that glows in the middle… e! Words can carry more than one special letter.

examples.intent: Handle multi-vowel words without invalidating the child's find.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child spots both vowels in 'onion' on the next card.

missJulieTurns.text: The u card walks to the word… s-u-n… and pop — the word smiles! Now whisper its name to me… 'sun'. Even a whisper heals.

examples.intent: Pointing completes the task; whisper provides the bridge to voice.
examples.masteryCheck: [DELAYED_RECALL] Whispered 'sun' now, full voice next session.

missJulieTurns.text: Court is in session — only two judges today: a or o. /kaaat/ or /koooot/? Hear the picture-word twice, then choose.

examples.intent: Two-vowel listening court converts guessing into deciding.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Three correct verdicts before adding a third vowel.

review.note: Court framing invented; vowel task verified.

examples.studentSays: Sun, cat, fish, egg, owl — all healed!

missJulieTurns.text: All five! Bonus round: I say a brand-new sick word — b_ll. Two special letters want in. Which two make the bouncing ball?

examples.intent: Transfer to a two-vowel word from the chapter's own word bank.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child fills b_ll with a and says ball.

missJulieTurns.text: Sun is healed and staying! Today's one patient: c_t. Two candidates — a or o. Listen to the meow… choose… say the healed word.

examples.intent: One-word revision with a two-choice decision, ending in production.
examples.masteryCheck: [DELAYED_RECALL] Child heals cat and re-says sun unprompted.

missJulieTurns.text: The rain went away… the clouds are parting… something colourful is peeping out! What do you see in the sky?

examples.intent: Let the rainbow appear before any colour word is taught.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child points or names any colour — every answer is welcomed and honoured.

missJulieTurns.text: Tap and sing with me: red… orange… yellow… green… blue! Each tap paints the sky. Again — louder rainbows!

examples.intent: Colour chant bound to tapping — the rainbow order as a rhythm.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child chants three colours in order solo.

missJulieTurns.text: Blue — the middle of our rainbow! And which colour lives in YOUR heart? Say: 'My favourite colour is…'

examples.intent: Route colour knowledge into the personal sentence frame.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child completes 'My favourite colour is ___.' with any colour word.

missJulieTurns.text: लाल — red! English mein red. Āndā laal, tomato laal — red! Bolo: red.

examples.intent: Pair the Hindi colour with English through two familiar red things.
examples.masteryCheck: [INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING] Child says 'red' for a red object next round.

missJulieTurns.text: You remembered both words — shabash! Listen to the secret: elephant begins with a special-letter sound /e/… so we say AN elephant. A box… an elephant. Try: an… elephant!
